questions.q: Why does the capstone build one vertical slice (a parent pays a term fee) end to end before anything else?
questions.explain: A vertical slice runs through HTTP, identity, tenancy, permissions, the provider, the database, events, jobs and observability at once. If those pieces fit together for the riskiest flow, the rest is incremental work with known acceptance criteria.
options: Because payments are the easiest feature to build
It crosses every layer where mistakes are expensive, so it proves the architecture works together, and everything else can be planned as milestones on top of it
Because ZudoJS requires the payment module to be registered first
So the admin screens can be skipped entirely

questions.q: Ada's phone sends the same payment request twice because of a weak network. What makes her be charged once?
questions.explain: Idempotency is a protocol between client and server (the key) and again between server and provider (the reference). The unique constraint makes it hold even when two copies race.
options: The rate limiter blocks the second request
The browser deduplicates identical POST requests

The Idempotency-Key header, stored with a unique constraint per school: the second request finds the first payment and returns it; and one level down, the same provider reference is never charged twice
The permissions engine refuses a second payment

questions.q: KoboPay does not answer within the timeout on any of the three attempts. What does FeesDesk answer, and why?
questions.explain: A timeout means "no answer", not "no". Reporting failure could make the parent pay again and be charged twice; reporting success could credit money that never arrived. Pending is the only honest state.
options: 500, because an error happened
402, because the payment failed
202 with the payment still pending, because the charge may or may not have happened; reconciliation settles it later
201, assuming the provider will succeed

questions.q: Why is the card charged between two transactions instead of inside one?
questions.explain: Rolling back a database transaction does not un-charge a card. So FeesDesk records "pending" first, charges, then settles in a second short transaction. A crash in between leaves a pending payment with a reference that reconciliation can finish.
options: The transaction manager forbids network calls

A transaction held open during a slow network call keeps its locks and connection for seconds, and a provider charge cannot be rolled back anyway; recording the intention before and the outcome after keeps both sides consistent
PGlite cannot run fetch inside a transaction
It makes the charge faster

questions.q: Two phones pay the full ₦450,000 for the same bill at the same moment. What stops the school receiving ₦900,000?
questions.explain: Subtracting pending payments is what closes the race: the first payment is not yet paid when the second request checks. The CHECK (paid_kobo <= amount_kobo) constraint is the last line of defence if the code is ever wrong.
options: The cache holds the bill for 60 seconds
The HTTP server handles one request at a time

The reservation: in one transaction, the bill is locked and the new payment is allowed only up to the amount minus what is paid and pending; the second request sees the first one pending and is refused
KoboPay refuses the second charge

questions.q: Tunde, from another school, tries to pay Ada's bill by changing the id in the URL. Why does he get 404 rather than 403?
questions.explain: requireAccess first asks whether the caller may read the bill. If not, it is "not found", exactly like a missing one. Only someone who can see the bill gets the more precise 403 for an action they may not take.
options: 403 is reserved for administrators
A 403 would confirm that the bill exists; answering 404 for bills the caller may not even see makes ids impossible to probe
The router cannot produce 403
Because the bill really does not exist in the database

questions.q: Which facts does FeesDesk take from the payment request itself?
questions.explain: Validation proves a value has the right shape, not that the caller is entitled to it. Identity and tenant come from the server's own session record; money owed comes from the database.
options: The school, the parent and the amount
The school and the price
Only the bill id and the amount (both checked); the school and parent come from the session, the price from the bill in the database
Everything, after schema validation

questions.q: Which KoboPay outcomes does chargeWithRetry retry?
questions.explain: Retrying a permanent failure wastes time and can hide a configuration bug; retrying a decline is rude to the parent's bank. The retryIf predicate encodes which failures are transient.
options: Every error, up to three times
Only declines, in case the card works the second time
Only a 503 and a timeout: failures that might pass. A decline is an answer, and a 401 from a wrong secret will not fix itself
Nothing; retries are the queue's job

questions.q: Why must all three attempts of one charge send the same reference?
questions.explain: In the provider example, the slow charge timed out three times and KoboPay still made exactly one charge. Idempotent references are what make retries safe for money.
options: The provider requires a reference on every call
An attempt that timed out may still have been charged; with the same reference the provider returns that charge instead of making a second one
It makes the logs easier to read
The rate limiter keys on the reference

questions.q: Why is fee.paid published after the settle transaction commits, not inside it?
questions.explain: Side effects follow facts. The remaining risk, a crash between commit and publish, is what an outbox table fixes (Milestone 3).
options: Events cannot be published inside async functions
Listeners queue receipts and clear caches; if they ran before commit and the transaction then rolled back, a receipt would go out for money that was never recorded
Publishing inside a transaction is slower
The event bus has no access to the database

questions.q: With a plain tx.afterCommit(…), the receipt job kept failing with "Transaction is closed". What was happening?
questions.explain: AsyncLocalStorage context flows into everything started from a callback, including timers and queued jobs. Running the callback through context.exit starts that work with no transaction in scope. It is reported as a defect of the published package.
options: The queue ran jobs before the commit
PGlite closes after every transaction
Work started from the afterCommit callback inherited the finished transaction's async context, so the job's queries and even a new manager.run joined the committed transaction
The job used the wrong school

questions.q: Why does a receipt job carry only { schoolId, paymentId }, and call identity.runAs(schoolId, …)?
questions.explain: Every piece of background work needs its tenant restored the way a request gets it from the session. Carrying ids instead of copies also means a retried job sees the latest state.
options: Queues can only store two fields
Jobs run outside any request, so there is no tenant context; the worker re-enters the school explicitly and reloads current data, so it can neither act on stale data nor leak across schools
To make the job faster
Because the parent's e-mail is secret

questions.q: The queue may run the receipt job twice (a retry after a crash). Why is that harmless?
questions.explain: At-least-once delivery is the norm; design handlers so a repeat changes nothing important. Deterministic keys are the cheapest way.
options: The queue guarantees exactly-once delivery
The storage key is fixed per payment (…/receipts/FD-1.txt), so a second run overwrites the same receipt; only the e-mail could be sent twice, which is acceptable for a receipt
The job checks a global lock
Receipts are stored in the cache

questions.q: What is the difference between /health and /ready in FeesDesk?
questions.explain: A load balancer routes by readiness; an orchestrator restarts by liveness. Mixing them makes a slow dependency restart healthy processes.
options: They are the same endpoint under two names
/health says the process is alive; /ready says it should get traffic: the lifecycle is ready, the database answers, and KoboPay's health check passes
/ready is only for the OpenAPI document
/health checks the database and /ready checks nothing

questions.q: The lifecycle starts database, then receipts and scheduler, then http. In which order does it stop, and why?
questions.explain: The acceptance suite proves it: a payment in progress during shutdown still answers 201.
options: The same order, so the database closes first
The reverse: http stops taking requests and finishes those in progress, then the workers drain, then the database closes, because each part still needs the ones below it until it is done
All at once, to be fast
Only http stops; the rest are killed with the process

questions.q: Why does app.ts pass { scope: ContainerScope.SINGLETON } to registerFactory?
questions.explain: Without the scope, billing would get a second identity service with its own tenant manager. Know the default of every registration you write.
options: Singletons are faster to type-check
A factory registration creates a new object on every resolve by default; services that hold state or connections must be built once and shared
The container refuses factories without a scope
It makes the objects immutable

questions.q: Reminders should go out at 08:00 in Lagos. Why is the cron expression "0 7 * * 1-5" with timezone: "UTC"?
questions.explain: This conversion is only safe because Lagos has no daylight saving. For a zone that changes its offset, you would need a scheduler with real time-zone support or a job that checks the local time itself.
options: Cron always uses UTC by definition
The published scheduler's cron trigger accepts only UTC or the server's own zone and throws for "Africa/Lagos"; Lagos is UTC+1 all year, so 07:00 UTC is 08:00 there
So the reminders arrive an hour early
Because weekdays start at 07:00

questions.q: The login limit test passed, yet the lesson calls the design bad. Why?
questions.explain: A test can pass and still describe the wrong behaviour. Count failures per account (school and e-mail), clear them on success, as in exercise 1.
options: Five attempts is too many
It counts every login per IP, successes included: parents behind one mobile network lock each other out, while an attacker spread over many IPs is not stopped
Rate limits should never return 429
The limiter leaks memory

questions.q: What does the cache key bills.greenfield.u-ada with the tag bills.greenfield achieve?
questions.explain: Tenant ids belong in cache keys for the same reason they belong in queries. (The first version used colons, which the cache refuses with a 400: its key parts allow letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores.)
options: It makes the cache shared between schools
Each school's and parent's list is cached separately, and a payment clears only its own school's entries through the tag
It encrypts the cached data
It stops the cache from expiring

questions.q: Why does a settled payment write two ledger rows, one positive and one negative?
questions.explain: A single "amount paid" column can drift without anyone noticing. Balanced entries make errors visible: a sum that is not zero means a bug.
options: To make the table larger
Double-entry bookkeeping: money moves from one account (fees receivable) to another (the provider's clearing account), and every school's ledger sums to zero, which is a check you can run at any time
One row per retry
PostgreSQL requires pairs of rows

questions.q: The process crashes right after the settle transaction commits and before fee.paid is published. What is lost, and what fixes it?
questions.explain: The in-memory bus forgets everything on a crash. The outbox makes "the payment is recorded" and "the event will be published" one atomic fact.
options: The money; a retry of the request fixes it
The receipt and the cache invalidation (the payment itself is safe); writing the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, published by a relay, fixes it
Nothing, events are stored by the bus
The ledger; a nightly job fixes it

questions.q: How does Greenfield allow instalments while Unity does not, without any if (school === …) in billing?
questions.explain: Per-customer behaviour belongs in configuration you can change and audit. The code only asks "is this allowed here?".
options: A column in the bills table
A feature flag with a tenant rule, evaluated with { tenantId: bill.schoolId }; enabling it for Unity is a change to the flag's data, not the code
Two copies of the billing service
A permission for each school

questions.q: What do 201, 202 and 402 mean for a payment response?
questions.explain: Distinct statuses let the client act without parsing text: show a receipt, show "we will confirm", or ask for another card.
options: Created, created later, and a server error
The payment succeeded; its outcome is pending; the card was declined
Three kinds of success
Validation error, conflict, and not found

questions.q: When is it safe for the reconciliation job to simply resend a pending charge?
questions.explain: Exercise 2 shows KoboPay returning the same ch_1 for the same reference. Check this property of every provider you integrate before relying on it.
options: Always
Never; it must refund and start again
Only when the provider is idempotent per reference, so resending returns the existing charge; otherwise it must look the charge up by reference and never charge again
Only between midnight and 6 a.m.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The same key with the same amount replays the first payment without charging; the same key with a different amount is a conflict; a new key is a new payment.
options: pay_1 pay_1 409 pay_2 2
pay_1 pay_2 409 pay_3 3
pay_1 pay_1 pay_1 pay_2 2
pay_1 pay_1 409 pay_2 4

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Succeeded payments are already in paidKobo; pending ones are subtracted too, because they may still succeed; declined ones hold nothing. A new ₦250,000 payment would be refused.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each payment writes a balanced pair. The clearing account holds what the provider owes the school, receivables went down by the same amount, and the whole ledger sums to zero.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The tenant rule serves true only for the listed tenants. Everyone else, including a call with no context at all, gets the default false: a missing context must never switch a feature on.
options: true false false
true true false
true false true
false false false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Client errors are exposed: their message is safe to send. A 503 from a dependency is not: the client gets a generic answer while the log keeps "KoboPay answered 503". In FeesDesk it never reaches the client anyway, because chargeWithRetry retries it.
options:
RateLimitError 429 true
AuthorizationError 403 true
ServiceUnavailableError 503 false

RateLimitError 429 true
AuthorizationError 401 true
ServiceUnavailableError 503 true

RateLimitError 400 true
AuthorizationError 403 true
ServiceUnavailableError 500 false

Error 500 false
Error 500 false
Error 500 false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only failures that might pass on their own are retried. A 401 means the secret is wrong; retrying it three times only delays the alert.
options: retry retry stop stop
retry retry retry stop
retry stop stop stop
retry retry retry retry

questions.q: Exponential backoff without jitter, starting at 50 ms, capped at 500 ms. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each retry waits twice as long, up to the cap. Real retries add jitter on top, so many clients do not retry at the same instant.
questions.code:
const delay = (attempt, base, max) => Math.min(max, base * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
console.log([1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((attempt) => delay(attempt, 50, 500)).join(" "));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A lookup table keeps the mapping in one place. The last value is a warning: a status the table does not know gives undefined, so when you add refunds in Milestone 3, add them here too, and let TypeScript's as const table catch the omission.
options: 201 402 202 undefined
201 202 402 undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Unknown fields are dropped, so a schoolId or a price in the body never reaches billing. The school comes from the session and the price from the bill.
options: true {"amountKobo":250000,"cardToken":"tok_visa"}
true {"amountKobo":250000,"cardToken":"tok_visa","schoolId":"unity","priceKobo":1}
false undefined
true {"amountKobo":250000,"cardToken":"tok_visa","schoolId":"unity"}

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A command's payload fields sit next to its type. The bus routes by type; a missing handler (RefundPayment) is only discovered at run time, which is why the acceptance suite exercises every command.
options:
school greenfield pays bill 1
true false

school undefined pays bill 1
true false

school greenfield pays bill 1
true true

PayBill
true false

questions.q: The cache accepts key parts matching /^[a-zA-Z0-9._\-]+$/. What does this print?
questions.explain: Colons and spaces are refused. Build keys from ids you control, never from free text, and include the school so two tenants can never share an entry.
options: false true false
true true false
false true true
true true true

questions.q: A simplified version of FeesDesk's checks, in the same order. What does this print?
questions.explain: Visibility is checked before anything else, so a caller who may not see the bill learns nothing, not even that their amount was too large.

questions.q: Write outstanding(bill, payments): the bill's amount minus what is paid minus every pending payment. Declined payments count for nothing.
questions.explain: Pending payments reserve their amount until they are settled or declined. Without that, two simultaneous payments could each see the full amount outstanding.

questions.q: Write isTransient(error) that returns true for errors worth retrying: statusCode 503, 504 or 429, or a name ending in TimeoutError.
questions.explain: 429 and 503 say "not now", 504 and timeouts say "no answer in time". A 400 or 401 will give the same answer however often you ask.

questions.q: Write once(key, operation): the first call with a key runs operation() and remembers its promise; later calls with the same key return the same promise, even while the first is still running.
questions.explain: Storing the promise, not the result, is what covers the simultaneous case: the second call arrives before the first finished. This is how a provider can honour an idempotency key under concurrency.

questions.q: Write entriesFor(payment) returning the two ledger rows of a settled payment: kobopay-clearing with the amount, fees-receivable with minus the amount. Print whether the rows sum to zero.
questions.explain: Each row carries the school and the payment, so the books can be checked per school and traced back to a payment. The zero sum is an invariant a test can assert after every scenario.

questions.q: Write delays(attempts, base, max) returning the waits between attempts for exponential backoff: attempts - 1 numbers, doubling from base, capped at max.
questions.explain: Three attempts need two waits. That is how chargeWithRetry's attempts: 3 reads: three calls in total, not three retries.

questions.q: Finish reserve(billId, amount) so that two simultaneous full payments cannot both be reserved: check the outstanding amount and record the pending payment with no await in between. Throw new Error("too much") when the amount is more than is left.
questions.explain: In one process, "no await between check and write" makes the step indivisible. In PostgreSQL the same guarantee comes from locking the bill row inside a transaction, which is what FOR UPDATE in reserve does.

questions.q: Write a login guard: attempt(account, passwordOk) returns 429 once an account has 3 failures, 401 for a wrong password (counting it), and 201 for a right one (clearing the count). Accounts are compared case-insensitively.
questions.explain: The success after two failures clears the count; three more failures lock the account, and even the right password is refused while locked. Kemi, on the same network, is never affected. A real version lets the lock expire, as createRateLimiter's window does.
